processing: Ripe pu-erh with a milky aroma. How the aroma gets there is rarely stated by sellers, so assume flavouring or scenting unless the seller says otherwise.
harvest_season: Not tied to a season, as is usual for flavoured ripe pu-erh.
appearance_dry: Dark brown leaf, as is typical of ripe pu-erh, with a noticeably sweet milky smell.
appearance_liquor: Dark red-brown, as with other ripe pu-erh.
taste_profile: The name promises a sweet, milky aroma on an earthy ripe base; little else has been reliably described.

brewing.notes: Brew as ordinary ripe pu-erh, with a quick rinse. Aroma from scenting usually fades after the first few steeps.

vintage_note: Usually sold without a stated year, by weight, as an everyday flavoured tea. It is not considered a tea for ageing; flavoured aroma tends to fade, so buy small and drink it fresh. A seller who gives the base tea and year and explains the aroma is worth more trust.
description:
Nai xiang pu-erh, 'milk-fragrance pu-erh', is ripe pu-erh sold on its sweet milky smell. Little is documented about it, and it does not appear to be a traditional tea with a defined recipe.

Sellers rarely explain the aroma. A milky smell this strong is unusual for plain ripe pu-erh, so treat it as a flavoured tea unless told otherwise, and do not assume it contains milk either.

Expect the usual earthy, smooth ripe base under a sweet creamy scent that is loudest in the first steeps. Brew it like ordinary shu, with a short rinse and steeps kept brief, and do not expect the aroma to last the whole session.

Ask what the base tea is and what makes the smell. If you want a naturally scented relative, sticky-rice pu-erh gets its scent from a real plant, and it is a clearer choice.
history: Little is documented about the origin of this tea or when the name came into use. It is known mainly as a retail product, not from historical records.
